title: (In-Person) Spring 2027 Teaching Assistant Institute (TAI)
description: The Graduate and Professional School and the Center for Teaching Excellence present the Spring 2027 Teaching Assistant Institute (TAI), designed to prepare graduate students for teaching in a college classroom. TAI is part of the Teaching Assistant Training and Evaluation Program (TATEP). Attendance is required for new teaching assistants and for those who have not previously completed TA training at Texas A&M, serving as recitation leaders, laboratory instructors, or full-responsibility lecturers. Attending a TAI session is one of three mandatory university requirements that must be completed to receive a TAI Certificate of Completion. The Institute is also open to members of the Texas A&M academic community interested in developing their teaching skills. Check-in begins at 8:00 AM, and the Institute runs from 8:30 AM to 4:00 PM. Lunch will be provided for this session. Please indicate any dietary preferences or restrictions during registration. Learning Outcomes: Participants will be able to... 1) Make classroom decisions following University policies (i.e., FERPA, VAWA, Title IX, ADA); Identify University resources to support their role as teaching assistants. 2) Determine the connection between learning outcomes and assessment; Determine a plan for self-assessment including evaluating effectiveness of performance as a TA. 3) Choose appropriate teaching strategies to achieve learning outcomes; Select appropriate delivery methods (videos, interactive technologies, lecture, etc.). 4) Utilize effective public speaking skills; Determine appropriate processes and methods for communicating with students. 5) Apply various assessment strategies and tools; Discuss methods to provide effective feedback; Develop an assessment and feedback plan. 6) Prepare guidelines that communicate course expectations; Identify strategies for addressing classroom incivilities (e.g., talking out of turn, cheating, aggressive behaviors). For additional information about the Institute, including details on all requirements and required online training, visit tx.ag/SpringTAI.

Grounded in practical experience and shared examples, this session provides attendees with the strategies, tools, and resources needed to build their confidence and expand their skillsets. title: NACADA Webinar: Practical Strategies for Trauma-Informed Advising
description: As advisors, students frequently reveal the traumatic events of their lives to us. Without professional licensure in mental health services, what should advisors do? For students to access resources that will address their mental health needs, they first need to reveal to a trusted person that they need help. For this reason, it is incredibly important for advisors to know how to use trauma-informed practices to create a safe space for all students to ask for help. At the basis of trauma-informed advising is intentionally enacting the 5 principles of trauma-informed care in our advising practice, including safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, and empowerment” “Harris & Fallot, 2001”. All of these principles are relational skills at their core, highlighting the importance of relational advising strategies when working with students who have experienced trauma. While the practice of trauma-informed advising is primarily relational, it is often difficult to know how to practically enact trauma-informed conversational strategies with students during high-stress advising moments. This session is ideal for advisors who desire to deepen their understanding of trauma and its impact on students, while learning powerful conversational techniques to better empathize with students in distress. Participants Will Be Able To: - Identify what trauma is, how it impacts our stress-response system, and signs of a student in distress. - Use conversational techniques such as validation, scaling questions, externalization, and parts language to empathize with students while also maintaining appropriate boundaries. - Enact practical strategies for taking a trauma-informed and person-centered approach in our work as advisors. - Make effective referrals to mental health services.

description: Large advising caseloads are an increasing reality across higher education, often creating tension between operational demands and advisor well-being. Drawing on experiences within an advising center serving undergraduate business students at a large public institution, presenters will outline scalable strategies that promote clarity, consistency, and shared responsibility. Participants will examine structured appointment models, including required versus optional advising touchpoints, as well as tiered advising approaches such as individual, group, and walk-in formats. In addition, the session will explore advising delivery formats that support accessibility and efficiency, with examples drawn from our in-person and email advising models. The webinar will further highlight the role of standardized documentation practices, centralized resource hubs, and clearly defined advising boundaries in reducing redundancy and preventing burnout. Emphasis will be placed on practical frameworks that can be adapted to institutions of varying sizes and resources levels. Participants will leave with actionable strategies for designing advising systems that balance efficiency with advisor well-being in large caseload environments. Participants Will Be Able To: - Assess structural factors within their advising units that contribute to inefficiency or advisor burnout in large caseload environments. - Design structured appointment models that align required advising touchpoints with institutional capacity and student needs. - Apply tiered advising approaches (e.g., individual, group, and walk-in formats) to improve scalability and resource allocation. - Develop cross-team support systems and standardized documentation practices that promote clarity, shared responsibility, and consistency. - Establish sustainable boundaries and operational practices that protect advisor well-being while maintaining high-quality student support.
